title: Clothes & Appearance
subtitle: Talk about your wardrobe, describe how people look and find the right size

lessons.title: La garde-robe
lessons.description: Name the clothes in your wardrobe, say what they are made of and choose between porter, mettre and s'habiller.

blocks.heading: Un vêtement, des vêtements
blocks.body: Un vêtement is one item of clothing; in everyday French people almost always use the plural les vêtements for clothes in general. Your whole collection is la garde-robe, and a single outfit put together for an occasion is une tenue. Most clothing words are masculine, but the very common ones you already know — la robe, la jupe, la chemise — are feminine, so learn each item with its article.

blocks.heading: Les accessoires et les chaussures
blocks.body: Accessories complete la tenue. Some are naturally plural because they come in pairs: les chaussettes, les gants, les baskets, les bottes. Shoes have their own size word — la pointure — while clothes use la taille. Note that une écharpe is a long warm scarf and un foulard is a light silk one.

blocks.heading: Les matières : c'est en quoi ?
blocks.body: To say what something is made of, French uses en + material with no article: en coton, en laine, en cuir, en soie, en lin. The question is « C'est en quoi ? » or « C'est en quelle matière ? ». You can also use de before a material in fixed phrases (une robe de soie), but en is the safe everyday choice.

blocks.heading: Three verbs, three jobs
blocks.body: Porter describes the state of having something on — it is what you see. Mettre is the action of putting a garment on, and it is irregular: je mets, tu mets, il met, nous mettons, vous mettez, ils mettent (past participle mis). S'habiller means to get dressed in general and is reflexive, so it needs me, te, se. Its opposite pair is enlever (to take one item off) and se déshabiller (to undress).

blocks.heading: Describing a garment: en, à and colour agreement
blocks.body: Use en + material for what it is made of, and à + detail for a feature it has: une chemise à manches courtes, une jupe à fleurs, un pull à col roulé. Colour adjectives agree with the noun (une veste verte, des chaussures noires), but two colours stay invisible: a colour formed of two words (bleu clair, vert foncé) and a colour borrowed from a thing (orange, marron) never change.

passages.title: La valise de Camille
passages.french:
Camille part une semaine en Bretagne et elle prépare sa valise.
Elle plie d'abord trois tee-shirts en coton et deux jeans.
Elle ajoute un pull en laine, parce que les soirées sont fraîches là-bas.
Son imperméable jaune est déjà sur le lit : en Bretagne, il pleut souvent.
Pour la plage, elle prend un short, un maillot de bain et des sandales.
Elle hésite devant ses bottes en cuir, puis elle les laisse à la maison.
À la place, elle met ses vieilles baskets, plus confortables pour marcher.
Dans une poche de la valise, elle range une écharpe et des chaussettes chaudes.
Sa sœur rit : « Tu emportes ta garde-robe entière ! »
« Non, répond Camille, j'emporte seulement une tenue par jour. »
passages.english:
Camille is leaving for a week in Brittany and she is packing her suitcase.
First she folds three cotton T-shirts and two pairs of jeans.
She adds a wool sweater, because the evenings are chilly there.
Her yellow raincoat is already on the bed: in Brittany it often rains.
For the beach, she takes shorts, a swimsuit and sandals.
She hesitates in front of her leather boots, then she leaves them at home.
Instead, she puts in her old trainers, more comfortable for walking.
In a pocket of the suitcase, she puts a scarf and warm socks.
Her sister laughs: "You're taking your whole wardrobe!"
"No," answers Camille, "I'm only taking one outfit per day."

lessons.title: Décrire quelqu'un
lessons.description: Describe someone's height, build, hair and face, and make every adjective agree correctly.

blocks.heading: La taille et la silhouette
blocks.body: To describe height and build, French uses être + adjective: il est grand, elle est mince. For a precise height you use mesurer: « Je mesure un mètre soixante-quinze. » If someone is neither tall nor short, say de taille moyenne. Be careful with gros — it is direct and can sound rude, so people often prefer rond or fort.

examples.french: Mon frère est grand et mince.
examples.english: My brother is tall and slim.

examples.french: Elle est de taille moyenne.
examples.english: She is of average height.

examples.french: Elle a une silhouette fine.
examples.english: She has a slender figure.

blocks.tip: French gives height in metres: « un mètre quatre-vingts » (1 m 80), often shortened in speech to « il fait un mètre quatre-vingts ».

blocks.heading: Les cheveux et les yeux : avoir
blocks.body: Hair and eye descriptions use avoir, not être: « Elle a les cheveux longs. » Notice that French says les cheveux, not mes cheveux, in this structure. Cheveux is always plural, so the adjectives take an s: les cheveux courts, bouclés, raides. For colour, hair words have their own vocabulary: blond, brun, châtain, roux, gris, blanc.

blocks.tip: Châtain is the very common French word for mid-brown hair — much more used than brun for describing hair colour.

blocks.heading: Donner une impression : avoir l'air, ressembler à
blocks.body: To soften a description, French uses avoir l'air + adjective (to look / to seem) and ressembler à + person (to look like someone). Both are extremely common. With avoir l'air, the adjective normally agrees with the person: « Elle a l'air fatiguée. » Ressembler always takes à: on ressemble à quelqu'un.

blocks.heading: The four forms of an adjective
blocks.body: A French adjective changes to match the noun: add -e for feminine, -s for plural, -es for feminine plural. If the adjective already ends in -e (mince, jeune, chauve), the feminine looks the same. If it already ends in -s or -x (gris, roux), the masculine plural adds nothing. Say the forms out loud: the feminine often makes a silent consonant audible — grand / grande, petit / petite.

examples.french: Il est grand. / Elle est grande.
examples.english: He is tall. / She is tall.
examples.note: the d is pronounced in grande

blocks.tip: With a mixed group of men and women, French uses the masculine plural: « Paul et Marie sont grands. »

blocks.heading: Irregular feminines and adjective position
blocks.body: Some endings change shape: -eux becomes -euse (sérieux / sérieuse), -f becomes -ve (sportif / sportive), -en becomes -enne (mignon / mignonne doubles the n), and a few are simply irregular: beau / belle, roux / rousse, blanc / blanche, long / longue, vieux / vieille. Most adjectives follow the noun (les cheveux bouclés), but a short familiar group goes before it: beau, joli, grand, petit, gros, jeune, vieux, bon, nouveau.

lessons.title: Dans la cabine d'essayage
lessons.description: Ask for your size, try clothes on in the fitting room, give an opinion and point at things with ce, cet, cette and ces.

blocks.heading: La taille et la pointure
blocks.body: Clothes have une taille and shoes have une pointure — never mix the two. French sizes are numbers (36, 38, 40…) but shops also use letters: S, M, L, XL, said in English. To ask, use « Quelle taille faites-vous ? » or the easier « Vous faites quelle taille ? ». You answer with faire: « Je fais du 40 » — note the du before the number.

examples.french: Vous faites quelle taille ?
examples.english: What size are you?

examples.french: Je fais du 38, mais ça dépend des marques.
examples.english: I'm a size 38, but it depends on the brand.

blocks.tip: Faire du + number is the fixed pattern for sizes, just like « je fais du 39 » for shoes.

blocks.heading: Dans le magasin : demander à essayer
blocks.body: In a shop, la vendeuse or le vendeur usually opens with « Je peux vous aider ? ». If you only want to browse, the polite answer is « Je regarde, merci ». To try something on you say essayer, and the little room is la cabine d'essayage. Remember the two magic words: « Est-ce que je peux… ? » and « Vous auriez… ? » for a very polite request.

blocks.tip: In France you normally greet with « Bonjour » before asking anything — going straight to the question sounds rude.

blocks.heading: Donner son avis : ça me va ?
blocks.body: Two verbs carry almost every opinion about clothes. Aller à quelqu'un means to suit someone: « Ça te va bien. » Plaire à quelqu'un means to appeal to someone: « Ce modèle me plaît. » Both put the person in front as an indirect pronoun (me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur). Add trop (too) or assez (enough) to fine-tune: trop serré, assez large.

blocks.tip: « Ça me va » has two meanings: "it suits me" (clothes) and "that works for me" (a plan). Context decides.

blocks.heading: Pointing at things: this / that / these / those
blocks.body: French has one family of demonstrative adjectives where English has four words. Use ce before a masculine noun (ce pull), cet before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h (cet imperméable, cet homme), cette before any feminine noun (cette jupe) and ces before every plural (ces chaussures). French does not distinguish "this" from "that" — ce pull can be either, and context does the rest.

blocks.tip: Cet and cette sound identical (set). Only the spelling tells you the gender, so learn the noun with its article.

blocks.heading: -ci and -là : this one here, that one there
blocks.body: When you really need to contrast two items in the shop, hook -ci (here, near me) or -là (there, further away) onto the noun with a hyphen: ce pull-ci, ce pull-là. In real conversation the French rarely bother with -ci; they say -là for almost everything, so « Je prends celui-là » is the natural way to point at a garment on the rail.

passages.title: Trois cabines et une décision
passages.french:
Samedi après-midi, Léa entre dans une boutique du centre-ville avec son frère Hugo.
« Bonjour, je peux vous aider ? » demande la vendeuse.
« Oui, je cherche une veste pour un mariage. Je fais du 38. »
La vendeuse lui donne trois modèles : cette veste bleue, cette veste beige et ce blazer noir.
Dans la cabine d'essayage, Léa essaie d'abord la bleue : la coupe est jolie, mais elle est trop serrée aux épaules.
La beige lui va bien, seulement le tissu la gratte un peu.
Enfin, elle sort avec le blazer noir et Hugo lève les yeux de son téléphone.
« Celui-là est superbe. Franchement, il te va beaucoup mieux que les autres. »
Léa regarde l'étiquette : cent vingt euros, mais il y a une réduction de trente pour cent.
« D'accord, je le prends. Et je garde le ticket de caisse, au cas où ! »
passages.english:
On Saturday afternoon, Léa goes into a shop in the town centre with her brother Hugo.
"Hello, can I help you?" asks the shop assistant.
"Yes, I'm looking for a jacket for a wedding. I'm a size 38."
The assistant gives her three styles: this blue jacket, this beige jacket and this black blazer.
In the fitting room, Léa first tries the blue one: the cut is pretty, but it's too tight on the shoulders.
The beige one suits her, only the fabric is a bit itchy.
Finally, she comes out wearing the black blazer and Hugo looks up from his phone.
"That one is gorgeous. Honestly, it suits you much better than the others."
Léa looks at the price tag: a hundred and twenty euros, but there is a thirty per cent discount.
"All right, I'll take it. And I'm keeping the receipt, just in case!"
